title: Water for the enemy
hookLine: in battle, Bhai Kanhaiya gave water to wounded soldiers of both sides, and the Guru told him to add ointment too
tomorrow: the needle for the next world
last: GURU GRANTH SAHIB — THE BOOK IS THE GURU NOW.

lines: THE ONE YOU ARGUE WITH MOST.
A WATER BAG ON THE BATTLEFIELD.
cards: Who is the person you argue with most? Online, at work, at the holiday table. Suppose that person were hurt, on the ground, asking for water, with your own side watching to see what you'd do.
That's today's story, the first of two short ones about the people around the Gurus. A battlefield near Anandpur, in the years of the sieges. Smoke, noise, men down on both sides.
And one Sikh walking through it all with a leather water bag on his back, kneeling, pouring, moving on. His name was Bhai Kanhaiya. And his own side was furious with him.

teach.b: As Sikhs tell it, Bhai Kanhaiya's seva during the fighting was carrying water to the wounded. But he didn't check uniforms. He gave water to the Sikhs who were hurt and to the soldiers attacking them, exactly the same.
Some Sikhs saw it and went to Guru Gobind Singh.
He's helping the enemy, they said. The men he revives will fight us again tomorrow. So the Guru called him in and asked: is it true?
Bhai Kanhaiya said yes, and gave the answer Sikhs have repeated ever since. On that field, he said, I don't see Sikhs and I don't see enemies.

teach.h: IN EVERY FACE I SEE YOU.
teach.b: In every face I see only you, my Guru. The Guru didn't scold him. He was pleased.
He handed him a box of balm, an ointment for wounds, and said: from now on, don't just give water.
Dress their wounds too. The Guru didn't just allow it.
He made it bigger. The Guru Granth Sahib has a line Sikhs connect to this story, where Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase, that no one is his enemy and no one a stranger; he gets along with everyone.

Tradition says Bhai Kanhaiya went on to found a community of Sikhs devoted to this kind of service, the Sevapanthis, and they still exist. When Sikhs tell the story today, they come back to the water bag.

how: Sikhs tell the story of Bhai Kanhaiya as a model of seva for everyone, and many Sikh relief groups today serve people in disasters and conflicts regardless of who they are.

o: the Sikh who gave water to friend and foe alike
a Mughal soldier who became a Sikh in battle
a Sikh general who led the defense of Anandpur

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: gave him balm for wounds too

s: the Guru told Bhai Kanhaiya to give water only to Sikhs
the Guru was pleased, and gave him balm to dress everyone's wounds too.
Bhai Kanhaiya said he saw the Guru in every face
he said he saw no friend or enemy on the field, only his Guru.
the community he founded has died out
the Sevapanthis, devoted to service, still exist.

games.q: you're the Guru. your Sikhs say Bhai Kanhaiya is reviving enemy soldiers who will fight again tomorrow. he says he sees your face in every one. what do you do?
o: order him to serve only your own side.
tell him to stop serving on the battlefield.
give him balm, and tell him to dress their wounds too.
games.why: the Guru didn't just allow it. he made the seva bigger: water, and balm for the wounds, for everyone.

practice: Bring back the person you argue with, and picture their face, not their opinions: their tired eyes, the way they look when they're worried.

Picture handing them a glass of water, nothing else, no debate, and notice what happens in your chest; resistance is fine, that's honest. Then, if you can, try to see what Bhai Kanhaiya said he saw in every face.

wordCard.voice: Bhai Kanhaiya. The Sikh who carried water to wounded Sikhs and enemy soldiers alike, saying he saw only his Guru in every face.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: the leather water bag Bhai Kanhaiya carried.

carryVoice: Your line: every face is his. Water for both sides, and balm too. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition on Bhai Kanhaiya at Anandpur and the founding of the Sevapanthis
